ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The University of Wisconsin-Madison Institutional Review Board determined that the study procedures were exempt from review.
The University of Wisconsin-Madison Institutional Review Board determined that the study procedures were exempt from review.

Participants were classified by menstrual cycle status during their most intense psychedelic experience: menstruating during the experience (n=15), menstruating but not during the experience (n=60), not menstruating (n=25), and male participants (n=69).
Participants were recruited in June of 2024 through Prolific Academic, a participant recruitment platform that frequently produces high-quality participation (Douglas et al., 2023).
table.formatted: Participants were recruited in June of 2024 through Prolific Academic, a participant recruitment platform that frequently produces high-quality participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Douglas et al., 2023)</ref>.

table.text: Participants were invited to complete a follow-up survey two months later and were then asked whether they had used psychedelics in the past two months.

In the present sample, no differences emerged when female and male participants were compared overall, whereas differences were observed across menstrual timing groups, suggesting that sex alone may not capture variability associated with menstrual cycle status.
Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation in the study.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. summary_table.ethics_statements: The University of Wisconsin-Madison Institutional Review Board determined that the study procedures were exempt from review.
live_data_statements: Participants were classified by menstrual cycle status during their most intense psychedelic experience: menstruating during the experience (n=15), menstruating but not during the experience (n=60), not menstruating (n=25), and male participants (n=69).
Participants were recruited in June of 2024 through Prolific Academic, a participant recruitment platform that frequently produces high-quality participation (Douglas et al., 2023).
Participants were invited to complete a follow-up survey two months later and were then asked whether they had used psychedelics in the past two months.

In the present sample, no differences emerged when female and male participants were compared overall, whereas differences were observed across menstrual timing groups, suggesting that sex alone may not capture variability associated with menstrual cycle status.
Electronic informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to participation in the study.

text.text: Background: Individual differences shape the acute subjective psychedelic experience, but menstrual cycle status remains an understudied source of potential variability.
Methods: In a longitudinal observational study, 169 participants reported psychedelic use during the two-month study period.

Participants were classified by menstrual cycle status during their most intense psychedelic experience: menstruating during the experience (n=15), menstruating but not during the experience (n=60), not menstruating (n=25), and male participants (n=69).

Primary analyses examined associations between cycle status and ego dissolution (Ego Dissolution Inventory; EDI), mystical-type experience (Mystical Experience Questionnaire; MEQ), and challenging experience (Challenging Experience Questionnaire; CEQ), adjusting for dose and age.
Exploratory analyses examined MEQ and CEQ subscales and post-acute risk of harm to self and others.
Results: Participants menstruating during their experience reported higher EDI scores than both those menstruating but not during the experience and male participants (β=-0.89 and -0.68, ps≤.011).
Cycle status was not associated with MEQ or CEQ scores.

Exploratory analyses found higher physical distress and death subscale scores among participants menstruating during their experience than among those menstruating but not during the experience (β=-0.77 and -0.80, ps≤.005).
Risk of post-acute harm to self and others was higher among those menstruating during the experience than among those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (OR=6.41, p=.022).
Conclusions: Menstrual cycle timing may be associated with aspects of the acute psychedelic experience, specifically ego dissolution and potentially risk of post-acute harm to self and others.
These preliminary findings support further investigation of menstrual cycle status in psychedelic research.
In recent years, clinical research on psychedelics has increasingly examined individual differences that shape the acute subjective psychedelic experience.

Studies have identified interindividual differences that impact the psychedelic experience including dose, personality traits, and demographic factors (Aday et al., 2021; Haijen et al., 2018; Hartogsohn, 2017).
text.formatted: Studies have identified interindividual differences that impact the psychedelic experience including dose, personality traits, and demographic factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Aday et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Haijen et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Hartogsohn, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Sex is increasingly recognized as one such factor.

For example, one recent study found that female participants reported greater subjective intensity following psychedelic use than male participants (Mason et al., 2026), suggesting that sex may moderate the acute psychedelic experience.
text.formatted: For example, one recent study found that female participants reported greater subjective intensity following psychedelic use than male participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mason et al., 2026)</ref>, suggesting that sex may moderate the acute psychedelic experience.

text.text: Despite this growing body of research, comparatively little attention has been paid to sexspecific physiology, including menstrual cycle timing and hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle.

Because many psychedelic compounds act through the serotonergic system (Nichols, 2016), and ovarian hormones are known to modulate serotonergic signaling (Bethea et al., 2002), hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle may contribute to variability in the acute subjective psychedelic experiences.
text.formatted: Because many psychedelic compounds act through the serotonergic system <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Nichols, 2016)</ref>, and ovarian hormones are known to modulate serotonergic signaling <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bethea et al., 2002)</ref>, hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle may contribute to variability in the acute subjective psychedelic experiences.

text.text: Therefore, understanding these factors is important for informing more personalized approaches to psychedelic research and treatment.
The acute psychedelic experience is multidimensional, encompassing both positive and negative valence.

In a longitudinal observational study of people who used psychedelics in naturalistic settings, we investigated whether menstrual cycle status at the time of participants' most intense psychedelic experience during the two-month study period was associated with three dimensions of that experience: ego dissolution, mystical-type experience, and challenging experience.
We also explored whether cycle status was associated with specific features of mystical-type and challenging experiences, and with overall risk of harm in the days or weeks following the experience.
Participants were recruited in June of 2024 through Prolific Academic, a participant recruitment platform that frequently produces high-quality participation (Douglas et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Participants were recruited in June of 2024 through Prolific Academic, a participant recruitment platform that frequently produces high-quality participation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Douglas et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Informed consent to participate was obtained electronically from all participants prior to their completion of baseline surveys.
The University of Wisconsin-Madison Institutional Review Board determined that the study procedures were exempt from review.
This study was part of a larger study (Simonsson et al., 2025) in which participants received payment for completion of their surveys.
text.formatted: This study was part of a larger study <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Simonsson et al., 2025)</ref> in which participants received payment for completion of their surveys.

text.text: At baseline, participants reported sociodemographic characteristics, including age.
Participants were invited to complete a follow-up survey two months later and were then asked whether they had used psychedelics in the past two months.
Of the participants who completed baseline and follow-up, 169 reported a psychedelic experience during the study period and formed the analytic sample.

Those participants who reported female sex assignment at birth were also asked questions about reproductive status, including pregnancy status, breastfeeding status, regular menstruation status, as well as whether they were menstruating at the time of their most intense psychedelic experience during the two-month study period.
Ego dissolution was measured with the 8-item EDI (Nour et al., 2016; item range 0-100; α = .92).
text.formatted: Ego dissolution was measured with the 8-item EDI <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Nour et al., 2016</ref>; item range 0-100; α = .92).

text.text: Mystical-type experience was measured with the 30-item MEQ (Barrett et al., 2015;  item range 0-5; α = .97), which comprises four subscales: mystical, positive mood, transcendence of time and space, and ineffability. Challenging experience was measured with the 26-item CEQ (Barrett et al., 2016; item range 0-5; α = .98), which comprises seven subscales: fear, grief, physical distress, insanity, isolation, death, and paranoia.

Challenging experience was measured with the 26-item CEQ <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barrett et al., 2016</ref>; item range 0-5; α = .98), which comprises seven subscales: fear, grief, physical distress, insanity, isolation, death, and paranoia.

text.text: Total and subscale scores were the mean of their items, with higher scores indicating a more intense experience.
At followup, participants also reported whether they had experienced thoughts or attempts to harm themselves or others in the days or weeks following their psychedelic experience.
All analyses were conducted in R (R Core Team, 2025).

Linear regression models were fitted with a four-level cycle status variable (menstruating during the experience, menstruating regularly but not during the experience, not menstruating, and males) as the predictor of interest, while EDI, MEQ, and CEQ total scores served as outcomes.
Separate models were run for the three outcome variables.
Menstruating during the experience was set as the reference category, and the covariates described below were included predictors.
To characterize potential differences across dimensions of the psychedelic experience, exploratory analyses were conducted using the MEQ and CEQ subscales.
FDR correction (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) was applied to the exploratory subscale models only, across the 11 subscales and separately for each of the three group contrasts.
text.formatted: FDR correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995)</ref> was applied to the exploratory subscale models only, across the 11 subscales and separately for each of the three group contrasts.

text.text: To derive standardized coefficients, the outcome variables were standardized (i.e., z-scored); all predictors (cycle status and covariates) were categorical and were left in their original coding.
Overall risk of post-acute harm was examined with logistic regression using the same predictors and covariates, with results reported as odds ratios.
Because harm was relatively uncommon, Firth's penalized likelihood logistic regression (Firth, 1993) was conducted as a sensitivity analysis.
text.formatted: Because harm was relatively uncommon, Firth's penalized likelihood logistic regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Firth, 1993)</ref> was conducted as a sensitivity analysis.

text.text: Because the group of participants who reported menstruating during the psychedelic experience was relatively small, a sensitivity analysis was also conducted in which the four-level menstrual cycle variable was collapsed into a binary variable comparing participants who were menstruating during the psychedelic experience with all other participants.
The same covariates and outcome measures were retained in these models.
Models were adjusted for dose (low, moderate, large, very large, extremely large) and age group (18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-50).
text.formatted: Models were adjusted for dose (low, moderate, large, very large, extremely large) and age group <ref type="bibr">(18-24, 25-34, 35-44, 45-50)</ref>.

text.text: These covariates were selected based on documented associations with the intensity of subjective psychedelic experiences and, for age, relevance to menstrual cycle status (Hirschfeld and Schmidt, 2021; Mason et al., 2026; Shadani et al., 2024).

text.text: In additional analyses, the same models were fitted with sex at birth (female vs. male) as the predictor in place of cycle status.
Of the 169 participants, 100 (59%) were female and 69 (41%) were male participants.

Among female participants, 15 (15%) were menstruating during their most intense psychedelic experience, 60 (60%) were menstruating regularly but not during the experience, and 25 (25%) were not menstruating regularly.
At follow-up, 3 female participants (3%) reported being pregnant and 2 (2%) reported breastfeeding (Table 1).

text.text: Participants who were menstruating during the psychedelic experience reported significantly higher ego dissolution scores than participants who were menstruating regularly but not during the experience (β = -0.89, p = .002) and male participants (β = -0.68, p = .011).
The difference from participants who were not menstruating regularly was similar in size but did not reach significance (β = -0.62, p = .050).
The standardized coefficients indicated moderate-to-large effects (Cohen, 1992).
text.formatted: The standardized coefficients indicated moderate-to-large effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cohen, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Menstruation status was not significantly associated with MEQ or CEQ scores (Table 2).
text.formatted: Menstruation status was not significantly associated with MEQ or CEQ scores (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: Compared with participants who were menstruating during the psychedelic experience, MEQ scores did not differ significantly for those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (β = -0.50, p = .075), those not menstruating regularly (β = -0.43, p = .176), or male participants (β = -0.47, p = .078).
Likewise, CEQ scores did not differ significantly for any comparison (β = -0.31 to -0.47, ps ≥ .09).
Overall, 29 participants (17%) reported thoughts or attempts to harm themselves or others in the days or weeks following the experience.

This post-acute risk of harm was reported by 7 of 15 participants (47%) menstruating during the experience, 4 of 60 (7%) menstruating regularly but not during the experience, 4 of 25 (16%) not menstruating, and 14 of 69 (20%) male participants.

Participants menstruating during the experience had higher adjusted odds of risk of post-acute harm than those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (OR = 6.41, 95% CI [1.35, 33.90], p = .022).
Differences relative to participants not menstruating (OR = 1.56, p = .60) and male participants (OR = 2.49, p = .17) were not significant.
Results were similar using Firth's penalized likelihood (Supplementary Table S3).

text.text: Exploratory subscale analyses revealed two findings that survived FDR correction (Supplementary Table S1).
text.formatted: Exploratory subscale analyses revealed two findings that survived FDR correction (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Relative to participants who were menstruating during the psychedelic experience, those menstruating regularly but not during the experience reported lower scores on the CEQ physical distress subscale (β = -0.77, p raw = .005, p FDR = .028) and death subscale (β = -0.80, p raw = .002, p FDR = .023).
Sensitivity analyses yielded results consistent with the primary analyses.

When the fourlevel cycle status variable was collapsed into a binary variable, participants who were menstruating during the psychedelic experience reported significantly higher EDI scores than all other participants combined (β = -0.74, p = .004).
Associations with MEQ (β = -0.48, p = .064) and CEQ (β = -0.37, p = .155) total scores remained nonsignificant.
Notably, in additional analyses comparing female and male participants, there were no statistically significant differences in any of the outcomes (Supplementary Table S4).
text.formatted: Notably, in additional analyses comparing female and male participants, there were no statistically significant differences in any of the outcomes (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: This study examined whether menstrual cycle timing was associated with key aspects of the acute psychedelic experience, namely ego dissolution, mystical-type experience, and challenging experience, in a longitudinal sample of people who used psychedelics in naturalistic settings.

Female participants menstruating during their psychedelic experience reported significantly higher ego dissolution than those menstruating regularly but not during the experience and male participants, with moderate-to-large effect sizes.
No significant associations were observed for mystical-type experience or challenging experience at the total score level.
Exploratory subscale analyses revealed that female participants menstruating during the experience also reported greater scores on physical distress and death subscales.

Female participants menstruating during the experience were also more likely to report thoughts or attempts to harm themselves or others in the days or weeks following the experience, although this difference was significant only relative to those menstruating regularly but not during the experience.
Previous research on sex differences in response to psychedelics remains limited, and available evidence has not allowed for strong conclusions regarding sex-dependent effects (Shadani et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous research on sex differences in response to psychedelics remains limited, and available evidence has not allowed for strong conclusions regarding sex-dependent effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Shadani et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, studies have rarely been designed to examine hormonal state or menstrual cycle stage as sources of variability in response to psychedelics (Cohen and Blest-Hopley, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, studies have rarely been designed to examine hormonal state or menstrual cycle stage as sources of variability in response to psychedelics <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Cohen and Blest-Hopley, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the present sample, no differences emerged when female and male participants were compared overall, whereas differences were observed across menstrual timing groups, suggesting that sex alone may not capture variability associated with menstrual cycle status.
The observed increase in ego dissolution may reflect a broader amplification of psychedelic effects during menstruation rather than a change only specific to self-experience.

The precise hormonal mechanism underlying this finding remains unclear, however, and future research incorporating direct measurements will be necessary to clarify it (Mason et al., 2026; Shoar et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The precise hormonal mechanism underlying this finding remains unclear, however, and future research incorporating direct measurements will be necessary to clarify it <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Mason et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Shoar et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Associations with mystical-type and challenging experience total scores were not statistically significant.
This pattern could indicate that menstrual cycle status affects some aspects of the acute psychedelic experience, such as ego dissolution, but not others.
However, a more likely explanation is limited statistical power, given the small number of participants menstruating during the experience.
Larger samples will be needed to determine whether menstrual timing relates to the intensity of the acute experience broadly or to ego dissolution specifically.

Female participants menstruating during their experience reported risk of post-acute harm more often (47%) than those menstruating regularly but not during the experience (7%), those not menstruating regularly (16%), and male participants (20%).

This difference was significant only for the comparison with those menstruating regularly but not during the experience, and it rests on a small number of events, so it should be treated as exploratory.
Still, if replicated, it would suggest that menstrual timing is relevant to the safety of psychedelic use, not only to the subjective experience.

Exploratory subscale analyses showed that female participants menstruating during the experience had higher scores on the CEQ physical distress and death subscales than those menstruating regularly but not during the experience.
Psychedelics serve as nonspecific amplifiers of ongoing mental and bodily states (Grof, 2008), and it is important to consider setting in this context.
text.formatted: Psychedelics serve as nonspecific amplifiers of ongoing mental and bodily states <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Grof, 2008)</ref>, and it is important to consider setting in this context.

text.text: Participants who were menstruating may have entered the experience with physical discomfort and a specific mindset, which psychedelics could have amplified into greater distress or more challenging content.
Another biological explanation is also possible.
Menstruation falls in the early follicular phase, when estradiol and progesterone are relatively low.
Such sex hormones modulate central 5-HT2A receptor binding in humans (Moses et al., 2000), and this phase may be associated with increased sensitivity to psychedelics (Kuypers et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Such sex hormones modulate central 5-HT2A receptor binding in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Moses et al., 2000)</ref>, and this phase may be associated with increased sensitivity to psychedelics <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Kuypers et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Neither explanation has been tested directly, and future studies should assess pre-experience mood and menstrual symptoms alongside hormonal measures.
An important limitation to note is the smaller sizes of the menstruating-during-experience group (n = 15) and the overall sample (n = 169).
As this provided limited statistical power, findings should be considered preliminary and interpreted cautiously.
Other limitations include the study's naturalistic, observational design, which relied on self-report for menstrual timing rather than direct confirmation via hormonal assays.
Given the observational design, causal claims regarding the link between menstruation and acute experiences cannot be made.
These limitations notwithstanding, this study suggests that menstrual cycle state at the time of a psychedelic experience may be associated with some acute subjective phenomena.
Future research should examine these associations in larger prospective samples and incorporate direct hormonal measurement across the full menstrual cycle.
Accounting for menstrual cycle status in future clinical trials may help clarify sources of variability in response and inform safer, more personalized psychedelic therapy.
